# Copper February 2010 

- February’s official 3-month prices were influenced more so by US dollar movements and economic data releases than by any fundamental factors.  A lack of clear direction in market sentiment was reflected in volatility reaching its highest level since August last year.  This was evidenced by daily min/max variations in official 3-month quotes ranging from -$330/t to +$232/t as of the 24<sup>th</sup> .  As a consequence of these volatile trading conditions, official quotes (3-month) ranged from the month’s low of $6260/t on the 5<sup>th</sup> to the month’s high of $7365/t on the 22<sup>nd</sup> . 

- Overall, we expect China’s net cathode imports to total ~2.4Mt in 2010, down by 23% from last year’s record level of ~3.1Mt.  The lower number reflects rising domestic refined production, some destocking and increased scrap availability.  During 2009, Chinese domestic refined production increased by 10.8% to ~4.2Mt.  This year, we forecast a further uplift of 10% to 4.7Mt (after adjusting for the expected availability of imported concentrates, blister and scrap). 

- Official consumption data for last year continued to be reported during the month.  As a consequence we have made a series of minor amendments to our 2009 estimates since our last report.  Despite the revisions the net effect on our global demand figure was minimal, and we estimate global refined copper consumption decreased by 3.1% to ~17.5Mt.  For this year and next we expect global demand to grow by 5.7%, to ~18.5Mt, and by 6.9% in 2011 to 19.7Mt. 

- Strong competition for trader tonnage and a flattening of the forward spreads have resulted in a marked decline in China’s spot concentrate buying terms, from $15/t & 1.5c/lb last month to $5/t & 0.5c/lb currently (i.e. broadly at parity with trader buying terms from miners).  In some instances, somewhat higher headline TC/RCs have been agreed along with more favourable side terms (to the seller).

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Volatile trading conditions remain** February’s official 3-month prices were influenced more so by US dollar movements and economic data releases than by any fundamental factors.

A lack of clear direction in market sentiment was reflected in volatility reaching its highest level since August last year.  This was evidenced by daily min/max variations in official 3-month quotes varying from -$330/t to +$232/t as of the 24<sup>th</sup> .  As a consequence of these volatile trading conditions, official quotes (3-month) ranged from the month’s low of $6260/t on the 5<sup>th</sup> to the month’s high of $7365/t on the 22<sup>nd</sup> .  The $1105/t trading range represented the largest spread since October 2008.  Thus far this month (as of the 24<sup>th</sup> ) official 3-month prices averaged $6847/t, down by 7.6% from January’s average of $7411/t. 

**Market sentiment dampened during the first week** On the downside, sentiment was dampened during the first week of the month by concerns over Greece’s ability to service its national debt, China’s additional measures to restrain bank lending and a surprise increase in US jobless claims.  As a consequence, official 3-month prices declined by $612/t (- 9%) between the 2<sup>nd</sup> and the 5<sup>th</sup> with quotes falling from $6873/t to $6260/t.  The Chinese news was particularly negative because it followed so closely after last month’s decision by the People’s Bank of China to increase its Reserve Requirement Ratio (RRR) by 0.5% to 16%.  Unconfirmed reports suggested that new bank lending for Q1 will be limited to RMB 2.4Tn which would represent 30% of the 2010 target.  If this is correct then this would indicate a significant slowdown in lending over the balance of Q1 given January’s provisional total of RMB1.6Tn.  The obvious ramifications of a marked reduction in credit availability and its impact on demand within the world’s largest copper consuming nation were a serious blow to market sentiment.  Meanwhile, the surprise increase in US jobless claims merely added to the growing concerns about the fragile nature of the recovery in the States. 

**Chinese return as strong buyers after New Year holiday** Market sentiment turned more upbeat once it became clear that Greece would be bailed out by its European neighbours.  This was further boosted by encouraging news from China. The country’s CPI data for January was lower than expected,  which, when combined with the recent slowdown in bank lending, led market participants to believe that the introduction of more austere credit tightening policies in the near-term was unlikely.  On the manufacturing side, preliminary figures suggested that Chinese January car sales reached a record high of 1.7M units.  This was up by 126% year on year and +17.7% month on month, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM).  Output continues to be boosted by incentive schemes which will run until the end of this year.  Also supportive were market reports which suggested that although visible exchange stocks were rising in Shanghai, stocks in bonded warehouses had fallen by ~50% since the start of the year and are now r

umoured to total around 100kt to 150kt. This significant reduction in bonded warehouse stocks, down to more manageable levels, was viewed as very encouraging for the market moving forward. These factors all helped to raise official 3-month quotes from the month’s low of $6260/t on the 5th to the month’s peak of $7365/t on the 22nd . Prices received an additional boost on the 22nd from the return of the Chinese after their week long New Year holidays. **Prices corrected lower in recent days** Since the 22nd official quotes have fallen and are currently trading around the $7100/t mark, prompted by a much lower-than-expected US consumer confidence figure for February. US consumer confidence fell to its lowest level since April 2009 amid rising job concerns. ### **Copper LME open interest vs copper price** 280000 8000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2010 Page 2 of 25 Copper Monthly Update **LME open interest highlights market uncertainty** Market uncertainty was highlighted by LME open interest data which showed mixed trading activity during the month. The fall in copper prices during January was driven primarily by the placing of new short positions. In February, however, the rebound was initially given life by fresh weight to the longs in the market, with funds flowing into copper as risk aversion waned. Rising prices in turn also appeared to trigger some short covering as some of those who had been shorting copper through January had to close out their positions. Although at the time of writing prices and open interest were higher than at the start of this month, the most recent price gains are as much due to short covering as new longs. This suggests a slowing in momentum behind the rebound. **Exchange stocks continue to rise** Total exchange stocks rose for the eighth consecutive month during February where net increases were seen on all three exchanges for the second consecutive month. As of the 25th total inventories rose by a net 54.5kt to 793.2kt, their highest level since December 2003. In terms of days of consumption total exchange inventories were the equivalent of 15.7 days, up from 14.6 days in January. The largest increase occurred in Shanghai where inventories rose by a net 48kt to 149.5kt (a seven year high) while on Comex stocks increased marginally by 0.1kt to 94kt. The China stock figure should be viewed in the context of that country’s recent holiday and it is therefore not surprising to have seen such an increase in these inventories. Meanwhile in the US, the small rise reflected ongoing sluggish demand from c

opper semis fabricators forcing traders to deliver unwanted material into warehouses. This was more noticeable in LME warehouses where net inventories into US locations rose by a net 17.9kt to 333.7kt. The main recipients were warehouses in Chicago (+1.6kt), New Orleans (+11.9kt) and St Louis (+2.1kt). Partly offsetting the increase in US warrants was a net 15.2kt decline in South Korean inventories to 90.3kt. As in previous months the net withdrawal reflected material destined for China where arbitrage opportunities remained positive during the month. Total LME stocks have increased by a net 6.2kt to 549.7kt, which is the equivalent to 10.9 days of consumption. However, on a slightly positive note, cancelled warrants continued to increase during the month and now stand at 19.5kt as of the 25th , up from 7.4kt at the end of January. **European spot levels remain firm** European premia held firm during the month with grade A material and Chilean cathodes from Rotterdam continuing to fetch around $80/t. Elsewhere, Italian warrants were unchanged at $75/t while standard grade cathode continued to trade around $20/t. Similar to last month, these healthy premia in Europe were due to the higher rates in China, rather than any underlying improvement in European demand. Spot cathode availability within Europe was also reduced by shipments or diversions of metal to China in order to benefit from the higher premia. Because of this, those consumers who chose not to commit to buying sufficient metal on a contract basis during the recent Mating Season are now forced to pay these higher levels. On this basis European premia are expected to remain firm, or indeed move higher in the coming weeks, despite there being no significant pick up in underlying demand. **Premia remain weak in the US** US premia remained unchanged at 3c/lb during the month. As noted earlier, US demand remains very weak with no significant recovery expected in the near term. In contrast, Chinese premia remained firm during February despite the New Year holidays. Premia have risen relative to the past two months, although in the run up to the New Year holiday there was a perceived, albeit moderate softening in terms to $90 to 100/t on a delivered China basis. Earlier in the month trades were recorded at closer to $100/t. However, post holiday quotes have strengthened and are currently trading around $110/t. As was the case in January, these elevated levels continue to be supported by increased demand for LME cathode because of the favourable prevailing SHFE price arbitrage. ### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 9000

> Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2010 Page 3 of 25 Copper Monthly Update **Chinese arbitrage remains favourable in February** China’s ongoing strength in demand has seen domestic prices continuing to trade above LME quotes during February. As of the 24th SHFE quotes (exclusive of VAT) had traded at an average $111/t above LME prices compared with an average of $145/t in January. This bodes well for Chinese refined copper imports in March and April, given that it typically takes 6 to 8 weeks between metal being booked and actually delivered to China. According to the latest customs data, Chinese refined copper imports in January totalled 197kt. While these were up by 9.1% from a year earlier they were also down by 19% from December’s level of 244kt. The month-on-month decline was not surprising given that some fabricators and financial institutions needed to use up their foreign currency credits before year end in order to maintain their credit limits in 2010. ### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 600 400

**Sharp fall in Chinese refined imports forecast in 2010** Overall, we expect China’s net cathode imports to total ~2.4Mt in 2010, down by 23% from last year’s record level of ~3.1Mt. The lower number reflects rising domestic refined production, some destocking and increased scrap availability. During 2009, Chinese domestic refined production increased by 10.8% to ~4.2Mt. This year, we forecast a further uplift of 10% to 4.7Mt (after adjusting for the expected availability of imported concentrates, blister and scrap). Also last year, direct use of scrap in the copper semis manufacturing sector declined by an estimated 20% due to a fall in imports (-28.5%), because of lower industrial activity within the developed economies. This year we forecast that direct use of scrap will increase by only 5%. We believe that availability of both new and old scrap will continue to be constrained by limited growth in industrial activity (new scrap) as well as demolition activity (old scrap) within the developed economies. At first sight the moderate forecast growth in direct use of scrap may seem at odds with our much lower forecast of refined imports in 2010. However, during 2009 there was somewhat of a disconnect between Chinese copper semis growth and the output of copper intensive products, especially those associated with the power sector, which accounts for 40% of overall Chinese demand. This was highlighted by the latest data from the National Bureau of Statistics which showed a 21% year-onyear increase in the production of copper semis during the first eleven months of 2009 compared

with 10% growth in power generating capacity. Even allowing for a strong uplift in the autos sector this still implies that there must have been a stock build in copper semis products during 2009 and this is reflected in our lower forecast of semis growth, which will impact China’s cathode imports this year. The combination of semis destocking, higher direct use scrap availability, the tailing off of investment projects associated with the incentive programme etc. means that our Chinese refined copper consumption growth (9% for 2010) is considerably lower than the massive uplift (+31%) seen in 2009. **Global market surplus forecast to fall significantly this year** Despite the lower forecast growth in Chinese refined copper demand this year, the 9% increase equates to a rise of ~0.6Mt in absolute terms and accounts for almost half of our 1Mt forecast increase in global refined consumption this year. Consumption outside of China still remains weak although there are signs that demand is beginning to pick up in some areas (see Consumption). However, we do not expect a sustainable recovery in the main economies outside of China until the latter part of the year. This year we forecast an increase of 5.7% (to ~18.5Mt) in global refined consumption, against global refined production growth of only 0.7% (to ~18.6Mt), giving a market surplus of ~100kt. This is down markedly from the ~1Mt surplus in 2009 and is reflected in our 2010 average price forecast of $7175/t ($3.25/lb) which is 39% up on last year. **Demand expected to recover fully in 2011** In 2011 global consumption is forecast to grow by a much stronger 6.9% as the effects of re-stocking outside of China become more evident. Refined production is forecast to grow by a healthier 5.3% but this will not offset the strong growth in demand. As a consequence, we forecast a market deficit of ~170kt. Metal stocks, in terms of days of consumption, will fall from the more normal level of 65 days in 2010 to 58 days. Prices should reflect this, rising by to an average of $7350/t ($3.33/lb). Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2010 Page 5 of 25 Copper Monthly Update ## Technical Analysis Prices moved down to $6,280/t on the 5th February before retracing much of this fall. Prices have subsequently fallen off 24% from the closing high of $7,432/t made on the 19th . Both $6,800/t and $7,130/t have offered support/resistance over the month. Critically the recent high has been lower than the prior high, and recent low at $6,300/t, lower than the prior low at $6,800/t reaffirming our belief that a major trend reversal downwards is increasingly likely. As we write, copper is critically poised just above potential support/resistance at $7,125/t which, again, coincides with the 50 day moving average. Over March we expect prices to move down to challenge the February low of $6,300/t, although prices may move up to the recent closing high of 7,440/t prior to this downwards move. On the downside support can be anticipated at $7,125/t, $7,000-6,900/t and at $6,800/t. On the upside resistance is expected at $7,440/t and at $7,660/t. 80 Relative Strength Index 80

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2010 Page 6 of 25 Copper Monthly Update ## Economic Developments **Inventory cycle drives US economic recovery** It has long been argued that the inventory cycle would act as a transitory but important driver of recovery in much of the developed world and recent data appear to strongly support this hypothesis. In Q3 2009, the effect of the inventory cycle is estimated to have contributed 0.7% to the 2.2% annualised growth recorded for the quarter. Preliminary estimates indicate that the US expanded at an annualised rate of 5.7% in Q4, the

strongest quarter-on-quarter growth in over six years. Of this 5.7%, as much as 4% is thought to have been driven by the inventory cycle with inventory stockpile liquidation falling from $139Bn in Q3 to just $20Bn in Q4. The question remains how growth will develop in 2010 as this transitory but powerful effect dissipates. ### **Inventories and sales in US manufacturing, seasonally adjusted** 600

### **Inventories to sales ratio** **The inventory cycle explained** As the world entered meltdown in Q3 2008, US manufacturing sales dropped sharply. This forced the ratio of inventories to sales to increase as producers found themselves with excess stock on their books. Given the intensity of the fall in sales and more importantly the contraction in order books (indicating future demand), producers decided to cut production and use inventories to supply their orders (see chart above). This aggressive destocking cycle commenced in September 2008 and continued through 2009. By mid-2009, inventories had been drawn down so much that producers needed to restart/ ramp up production to fulfil demand (albeit low) which triggered a surge in month-on-month production growth. The impact of this ‘inventory cycle’ is difficult to estimate ex-ante. Having driven more than half of the recovery in US GDP to date, it has surprised many on the upside. The question is, how long Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2010 Page 7 of 25 Copper Monthly Update will this effect last? Wood Mackenzie believes the US has already benefited from much of this inventory cycle and expects the effect to dissipate quickly through the first half of 2010. **Start of a period of restocking?** US manufacturing inventories are back to lows not seen since mid-2006 and have actually increased marginally in two of the last three months on an absolute basis. Does this mean we are the start of a period of inventory rebuild – with positive implications for economic growth in 2010? We think not for several reasons. First, while inventories are low, the inventory to sales ratio remains above average (for the decade up to September 2008) suggesting that there remains plenty of slack in the supply chain to fulfil current demand. There is therefore little incentive to restock until sales pick up significantly. Second, the effects of this recession are expected to have a lasting effect on the behaviour of businesses. In the run up to

the financial crisis, a number of manufacturers’ were running a high volume business with high inventory levels. This included the auto industry. These producers were left with significant levels of excess stock when demand collapsed, and also high fixed costs/ overheads that could not be offset against lower production. At the start of 2010, inventories had fallen 39% from a year earlier, contracting from 94 days of consumption to just 53. Many producers have stated that they do not intend to return to their pre-crisis models which proved so costly, and will instead be tailoring production to sales going forward. In an environment where small to medium sized businesses still struggle to get credit, running lean inventories and tailoring output to demand will likely be an attractive option. **US Industrial outlook** Month-on-month industrial production in the USA rose by 0.9% in January thanks to strong growth in auto production and inventory stabilisation. Industrial production is now up 5.5% from its nadir of June 2009. As discussed above, with inventories now stabilising, the inventory cycle contribution to industrial production growth in the coming months is likely to be capped by the growth in underlying demand. We also caution against reading too much into preliminary signs of recovery in business investment because of the low base it is starting from. Coupled with stubbornly high unemployment (likely moving back above 10% through 2010), overall growth in 2010 is expected to slow from the high rate enjoyed in H2 2009. As such, we continue to expect the pace of recovery in US industrial production to slow as we move into the second quarter. ### **Euro zone PMIs** 65 Manufacturing Output 1.4

**Euro zone outlook** In Europe, the recovery in industrial production may have stalled already. Activity in the euro zone unexpectedly contracted by 1.7% month-on-month in December, and remained down by 4.8% year on year. Capital goods production was particularly weak but data also suggest the inventory cycle boost is losing momentum. Leading indicators also point to a reduction in the future inventory boost to output. The ratio of manufacturing producer stocks to new orders has often lead changes in output: new orders continue to rise but the ratio has flattened, suggesting the initial inventory boost to production has already occurred. It also suggests that changes in future production will mirror changes in orders, and thus underlying demand. This is a real concern, as rising unemployment is weighing on private spending in Europe and growth prospects with key trading partners look limited because of low exposure to growth

in emerging markets. Once the effects of fiscal stimulus dissipate, the outlook for the euro zone looks bleak.  For these reasons, we expect growth in European industry to be precarious over the coming months – at best.

## Consumption 

**Official figures for 2009 continue to be reported** Official consumption data for last year continued to be reported during the month.  As a consequence we have made a series of minor amendments to our 2009 estimates since our last report.  Essentially we have lowered our demand figures for Africa and Latin America but raised our Asian and Western European estimates.  Despite the revisions the net effect on our global demand figure was minimal, and we estimate global refined copper consumption decreased by 3.1% to ~17.5Mt.  For this year and next we have lowered our global numbers by 22kt and 33kt respectively, reflecting the knock-on effect of the amendments made to our 2009 estimates, and now expect global demand to increase by 5.7% this year, to ~18.5Mt, and by 6.9% in 2011 to 19.7Mt. 

**Aurubis report firm pick-up in wire rod production during Q4 last year** The increase in our 2009 Western European copper demand estimate reflected a pick up in European wire rod production during the final quarter of last year.  This was highlighted by Aurubis who recently reported an 8.8% increase in its wire rod production during Q4 from a year earlier.  According to the company the positive result reflected increased market share, following the closure of the Chauny wire rod plant in France, as well as an improvement in underlying demand.  One wire rod producer explained that there was concern that the momentum experienced towards the latter part of 2009 reflected re-stocking ahead of the holiday period.  However, latest anecdotal evidence suggested that the upward momentum was carried through into January and February where some wire rod producers continued to report high shipment levels.  Unfortunately the pick up in the production of copper wire rod was not universal across the region where Northern Europe fared better than Southern Europe, according to our sources. 

**Supply difficulties in Italy** Wire rod production in Italy this month was hampered by cathode shortages.  Shipments across Europe into Italy were held up in Greece because of the industrial action that broke out mid-month with custom workers.  As a consequence, a number of cars and trucks were stranded at the country’s northern posts with Macedonia and Bulgaria because of the border posts operating with skeleton staff.  In addition, tolling business at one wire rod plant was disrupted because of delayed vessels from Chile.  While the eventual arrival of the delayed vessels from Chile will help ease the tightness, supply difficulties are not expected to be completely resolved any time soon. 

**Power sector continues to support European wire rod demand** F

irm orders from the energy sector remained the main support for wire rod demand this month. Our sources reported that the power sector has withstood the economic crisis well up to now, helped by the ongoing investment in the renewable energy sector. More recently, the market for harness wire has picked up, reflecting the recovery in the European auto sector. According to statistics from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association, total auto production increased in all of the major European economies, barring France, during Q4 last year from a year earlier. Auto production in Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK increased annually by 11%, 25%, 28% and 11.2% respectively in Q4 last year. ### **Production and shipments of copper wire rod and copper semis – (kt)** ||**2007**|**2008**|**2008**

One European wire and cable manufacturer, whose product is mainly aimed at the construction sector, reported a 30% decline in production between October 2008 and October 2009 when the downturn in construction activity was at its steepest. During the final quarter of last year and into January this year, the wire and cable manufacturer witnessed an improvement in demand. However, during February order levels slowed once more, while the outlook for March remains uncertain too. The wire and cable manufacturer explained that he sells his construction wire and cable to stockists, whose purchases are heavily influenced by the price of copper. While the stockists trade as a g

roup, the nominated chief buyer determines when purchases are made. Presently, the chief buyer expects that prices will fall because of rising stock levels, which goes some way to explaining the poor off-take seen in February and the uncertainty surrounding order levels in March. However, this is only a short-term view. Longer-term demand from the stockists is expected to recover more strongly as the need for pipeline supplies to be replenished takes hold. **Strong copper shape demand** Despite ongoing weak activity within the European construction sector, demand for copper shapes is reported to be very strong, which has surprised some producers. The recovery started during Q4 last year, and allowed Aurubis to report a 6.4% year on year increase in the output of its copper shapes. The improvement reflected the company’s concentration on shapes production at its Hamburg site as well as the launching of new products. Our sources inform us that this momentum was carried through into January and February, which have seen order levels that are reported to be above budget for some manufacturers. One manufacturer explained that the pick up reflected increased market share, which stemmed from some of the manufacturer’s competitors experiencing quality issues with their billet casting, as well as strong overseas demand. The latter was highlighted by recent figures from Assomet, Italy’s Non Ferrous Association, which showed that the production of copper bars and sections, sheet, strips and discs and tube fell by a combined 17.6% last year to ~123kt. The Association reported that the production of copper semi products, which included both copper and copper alloy products, fell by 20.6% last year to 937kt. This was considerably below the more normal annual level of 1.3Mt. Taking this into account we estimate that Italian refined copper consumption fell by 22% last year to ~500kt. This year we expect a small recovery of 2% that will come largely alongside the region’s general economic recovery. However, in Northern Europe we anticipate stronger growth rates in both Germany and Belgium as both countries will benefit from increased wire rod demand in light of the recent closure of the Chauny wire rod plant in France. Reflecting this we forecast that German refined copper consumption will increase by 5% this year, to ~1.1Mt while in Belgium demand will improve by 6.7% to 270kt. For Western Europe as a whole we forecast that refined copper consumption will grow by 2.1% this year to ~2.7Mt. ### **Shipments of USA copper and copper alloy products – (kt)** 20 550

**US economic activity continues to recover.** US manufacturi

ng activity rose significantly in January to its highest level since August 2004.  This was reflected in industrial production in the same month rising by 0.9% from a year earlier. This was the first annual gain since March 2008 and resulted in capacity utilisation reaching 72.6%.  However, while this represented the highest level since December 2008 it was still considerably below the pre-crisis peak of 79%.  Reflecting the positive data readings, auto production rose by 9.4% in January from a month earlier.  On an annual basis auto output was up a substantial 100.2% but this was from a very low base.  Also, production schedules for this month suggested that auto output will trend lower during February.  While auto producers are currently operating with much leaner inventories, 53 days of consumption versus 94, they have no inclination to return to the pre-crisis model which proved so costly when demand fell sharply.  Instead, auto production will be tailored to match sales.

**January housing starts misleading** In the construction sector, housing starts in January rose by 2.8% from a month earlier and 21.1% year on year.  However, as with the auto sector, the annual gain in starts was from a very low base.  At 591k units, housing starts remained well below the average level of 1M units, although the data did suggest that the decline in housing starts was stabilising.  This sentiment was reiterated by a copper tube producer who reported that the slowdown in copper tube demand had now levelled off, but they do not expect any recovery in tube orders until either Q3 or Q4.  For 2010 as a whole the producer expected his order levels to be little changed from 2009.  A cathode producer we spoke to also shared this view and confirmed that market conditions remained very weak.  He also added that some of his trader customers, who were contracted to take monthly shipments, were being forced to deliver this material to US warehouses because there was no demand for the metal from the copper semi fabricators.  Reflecting this we forecast that US refined copper consumption will increase by only 0.8% this year to ~ 1.6Mt, after an estimated drop of 21.2% in 2009. 

**Brazilian demand to recover strongly** Future demand prospects for Brazilian copper demand are very positive, after an estimated drop of 20% in 2009 to ~310kt.  The decline, brought about by the general downturn in the global economy, reflected copper product sales falling by 15%, according to Brazil’s non ferrous association, Sindicel.  However, this year the Association expects that demand will recover strongly, with product sales not far off 2008 levels.  Driving this demand will be strong growth in the auto sector, helped by increased exports, as well growing investment within the construction sector, especially on the commercial side.  The Association reported that the construction of three muc

h needed subway lines in Sao Paulo, as well as rail projects in other large cities, will support demand in 2010 and further forward. With this in mind we forecast that Brazilian refined copper consumption will increase by 8.4% this year to ~340kt. **Construction weakness cuts Japanese copper semis production in 2009** Although Japan’s manufacturing sector has shown some signs of life in recent months, the same cannot be said about its construction sector. In terms of residential construction the best that can be said is that it seems to have stabilised at a low level. Housing starts in December rose in month on month terms for the fourth consecutive month. Despite this improvement, starts still fell by 15.7% in year on year terms, and for 2009 starts totalled 788.4k units, a decline of 24%. The contraction in the Japanese economy, and the automotive and construction sectors in particular, weighed heavily on the country’s copper and copper alloy semis producers. According to Japan’s Copper and Brass Association, while production improved in the final months of last year, output for 2009 as a whole totalled just 654kt, a year on year decline of 30.7%. **Copper semis output in January reaches late 2008 level** On a positive note, demand for copper and copper alloy products recovered well at the beginning of the year. According to Japan’s Copper and Brass Association, the production of copper semi products increased by 55.2% year on year in January to 71.368kt, it’s first time above 70kt since October 2008. While the strength of the recovery was encouraging, it should be noted that the recovery was from a very low base. Also, the month’s total was still down 14.7% from January 2008 when production was more normal levels. The increase in the production of copper and copper alloy products in January was supported by the ongoing recovery in the Japanese auto sector where auto sales increased by 24.9% year on year in the month. However, at the time of writing it was still unclear what the impact will be on future demand for copper and copper alloy products from the auto sector, following Toyota’s recent woes. There is concern that the recalls on so many models will damage the company’s reputation indefinitely. ### **Japanese production of copper and copper alloy products – (kt)** 20 350

According to the Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association shipments in January rose 2.5% from a year earli

er.  This represented the first annual increase since September 2008.  However, likewise with the semis industry the improvement was coming from a low base. According to government statistics auto production in January last year fell by 41%% year on year to 577k units.  While demand for both copper and copper alloy products and copper wire and cable started the year on a positive note, production levels are still significantly below the more normal levels achieved in 2008. **Strong Chinese demand growth remains** Although the Chinese authorities are moving to slow the pace of growth during the course of 2010 and unwind some of the impact of their stimulus measures, the gradual recovery of export demand for Chinese copper-intensive goods will counteract the negative impact that this will have on copper demand. This was underlined recently by Chinese copper semis producers who reported that they expected demand for their products to continue rising after the Chinese New Year holiday, despite the government’s recent moves to tighten credit availability.  One copper plate and strip producer reported that he expected demand to increase during the industry’s peak season in March and April.  This was reconfirmed by a copper tube producer who announced that his production was running at full capacity during February, where orders in March were also expected to be strong.  With this in mind we continue to forecast that Chinese refined copper consumption will increase by 9% this year to ~7.3Mt.  As noted earlier in the report, this is down sharply from last year’s growth of ~31% but, in absolute terms, the increase is still significant.

## Production news 

**Several mine disruptions noted in February – impact on production as yet unclear** February has seen a number of mine disruptions including industrial action in Portugal and two Zambian mines being forced to close, albeit it temporarily, due to a power supply failure.  The Zambian operations affected were First Quantum’s 250kt/a Kansanshi mine and Equinox’s 170kt/a Lumwana mine which are located on the western extreme of the Zesco grid.  The outage occurred after a 330KV tower was brought down by vandals leaving the two mines without power for three and a half days.  While neither company has quantified how much production was lost during the outage the Chinese owners of the nearby Chambishi smelter introduced a temporary

_force majeure_ on blister deliveries to customers on account of these mine disruptions.  Elsewhere, underground workers at the 90kt/a Neves Corvo mine are staging two-hour strikes at the start of each shift and are calling for an increase in salaries of around 17%.  This follows above-inflation pay rises that were granted to the workers in January.  Lost production is difficult to calculate at this stage given that surface ore stockpiles are being used to supplement lower run of mine output. 

**Codelco records a 15% rise in commercial copper output** Codelco recorded a 15% year-on-year increase in its 2009 commercial copper production, from 1547.6kt to 1782.4kt (including the company’s 49% stake in El Abra).  Codelco Norte produced 874.7kt (755.3kt in 2008), Salvador 65.5kt (42.7kt), Andina 209.7kt (219.5kt), El Teniente 404.1kt (381.2kt), Gabriella Mistral 148kt (67.7kt) and El Abra 80.4kt (81.2kt).  Separately, during a ceremony to receive the first shipment of natural gas at the Mejillones LNG terminal, Chilean president, Michelle Bachelet announced that studies carried out by Codelco will enable the useful life of the company’s Salvador division to be extended from the previouslyplanned closure of end 2011 until at least 2021.  The mine, which has been in production since 1959 currently produces around 50kt/a of copper-in-concentrates and a further 20-25kt/a of SxEw Cu (including output from third party material). Many factors have changed since the original closure decision was taken in 2005, not least the long-term copper price outlook.

Copper Monthly Update 

Cananea is capable of producing ~125kt/a of copper-in-concentrates and 45kt/a of SxEw Cu.  The mine has not operated since April 2008 and we have assumed for this year that it will produce 30kt of copper-in-concentrates and 10kt/a SxEw Cu. 

**Kazakhmys eyes 2014 start up of its Boschekul project** Kazakhmys expects to bring on stream its 100kt/a Boschekul project in Kazakhstan’s north-eastern Pavlodar region in 2014.  Last year the company borrowed $2.7Bn from the China Development Bank and the Joint Stock Company Sovereign Wealth Fund Samruk-Kazyna and will allocate approximately 75% of this towards developing Boschekul.  Current plans envisage a 25Mt/a conventional open pit mining/milling complex and for the concentrates to be railed to the company’s Balkhash smelter. 

**Freeport resumes concentrate production at Morenci** Freeport McMoran Copper and Gold is to resume sulphide ore mining and milling at its Morenci mine during Q2 2010.  Operations were suspended in early 2009 on account of low copper prices.  The reactivation is likely to have been sanctioned partly on account of the more favourable price environment and also to maximise sulphuric acid production from the company’s Miami smelter which appears to be in relatively short supply in the region.  Morenci’s copper-in-concentrate production is forecast to be approximately 20kt this year, rising to 40kt in 2011.  Separately, Freeport will hire an additional 200 to 250 employees at its Miami SxEw operation where a $40M investment programme will see production ramped up to 45kt/a Cu by H2 2011. 

**Anvil Mining reports good progress at Kinsevere project** Anvil Mining reports good progress at its Kinsevere SxEw project in the DRC which is currently at an advanced stage of construction.  In Q3 2009 Anvil entered into a strategic alliance with Trafigura, with the trading company taking up a 36% equity investment in Anvil at a cost of $100M with a further $100M extended to Anvil in the form of a committed debt facility.  Proven and probable reserves at Kinsevere currently amount to 20Mt grading 3.8% Cu which are sufficient to sustain a mine life of ten years.  Additional identified resources amount to almost 24Mt at similar grades. 

**Mopani to invest in new shaft at Nkana mine** Mopani Copper Mines plans to invest $100M at its Nkana underground mine in order extend the mine’s life by 25 years.  Starting this year, a new shaft will be sunk to access approximately 100Mt of ore that lies beneath the existing Nkana south and central shaft ore bodies. 

**KCM to reprocess old Nkana slag at Konkola** KCM is to reprocess a 3Mt smelter slag dump containing ~2% Cu.  The company will engage a contractor to truck the crushed slag some 90km to the Konkola mill where it will be processed at a rate of 3kt/

d.  This equates to additional copper-in-concentrates from this source of ~15kt/a. 

**Boliden to commission Aitik expansion in April** Boliden reports that the first production line in the new concentrator at its Aitik mine is expected to be commissioned on April 1<sup>st</sup> 2010.  For this year Aitik’s ore production is expected to total 31Mt, rising gradually to full capacity (36Mt) in 2014.  Copper-in-concentrate output should increase from 46kt last year to ~70kt/a during the initial years of the expansion. 

**Teck lowers production forecasts for Highland Valley** Teck has developed a preliminary plan to address the recent geotechnical issues in the Valley pit at its Highland Valley complex. This two-year plan includes approximately 75-80Mt of additional stripping and a comprehensive dewatering and buttress placement plan to stabilise the east wall.  Higher grade portions of the Valley pit will be restricted during this time, although this shortfall in ore availability is expected to be partially made up with ore from the Lornex and Highmont pits.  The overall blend of ores available for processing are expected to have lower grades, throughput rates and recoveries.  The latest guidance from Teck is that Highland Valley’s production will be approximately 100kt and 105kt in 2010 and 2011 respectively.  After 2011, copper production is expected to average 125kt/a over the current mine life. 

**Sale of Tsumeb smelter to Dundee Precious Metals approved** The Namibian Competition Commission has approved Weatherly’s sale of the Tsumeb smelter to Dundee Precious Metals.  In January, Dundee entered into a conditional agreement to acquire the smelter for ~$33M plus other obligations.  Tsumeb is one of the very few smelters that can handle copper concentrates containing exceedingly high concentrations of arsenic and actually recover the arsenic as a saleable by-product.  Dundee’s Chelopech mine in Bulgaria produces concentrates containing 5-6% As which have proved fairly difficult to market historically.  The company began shipping concentrates to Tsumeb in 2007 and Dundee and Louis Dreyfuss loaned Weatherly $11.3M to expand Tsumeb to cater for more Chelopech and Marcapunta (Peru) concentrates (the latter’s concentrates are also high in arsenic).  Dundee had hoped to construct a pressure leaching facility in Bulgaria to eventually treat the Chelopech concentrates, however, difficulties over permitting etc. forced the company to consider alternative long-term smelting arrangements.  A new oxygen plant has just been commissioned at the Tsumeb smelter and the capacity of the plant will be raised from 100kt/a to 240kt/a of concentrates (i.e. to ~45kt Cu). 

**New multi-metallic smelting complex at Yanbu under evaluation** Tasnee, a Saudi Arabian industrial group, along with its partner Nabaa Industrial Development and Investment Co. are undertaking feasibility work on a multi-metallic smelting complex at the sea port of Yanbu.  Initial plans call for

the complex to produce 100kt/a of copper, lead and zinc, rising to 200kt/a per metal in a phase II expansion. As regards timing the companies are aiming for 2013. Various projects have been considered at Yanbu previously due to the cheap cost of gas and labour. However, this is the first project that encompasses multiple metals.
